[[File:Neuron3.png|thumb|right|400px|Fig. 1. Neuron and myelinated axon, with signal flow from inputs at dendrites to outputs at axon terminals. The signal is a short electrical pulse called action potential or 'spike'.]]
[[File:Spike HH 2.png|thumb|Fig 2. Time course of neuronal [[action potential]] ("spike"). Note that the amplitude and the exact shape of the action potential can vary according to the exact experimental technique used for acquiring the signal.]]
'''Biological neuron models''', also known as '''spiking''' '''neuron models''',<ref name="Gerstner_2002">{{cite book | vauthors = Gerstner W, Kistler WM |title=Spiking neuron models: single neurons, populations, plasticity|date=2002|publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=0-511-07817-X|location=Cambridge, U.K.|oclc=57417395}}</ref>  are mathematical descriptions of the conduction of electrical signals in [[neuron]]s. Neurons (or nerve cells) are [[Membrane potential|electrically excitable]] cells within the [[nervous system]], able to fire electric signals, called [[action potentials]], across a [[Neural network (biology)|neural network.]] These mathematical models describe the role of the biophysical and geometrical characteristics of neurons on the conduction of electrical activity.

Central to these models is the description of how the [[membrane potential]] (that is, the difference in [[electric potential]] between the interior and the exterior of a biological [[Cell (biology)|cell]]) across the [[cell membrane]] changes over time. In an experimental setting, stimulating neurons with an electrical current generates an [[action potential]] (or spike), that propagates down the neuron's [[axon]]. This axon can branch out and connect to a large number of downstream neurons at sites called [[synapse]]s. At these synapses, the spike can cause the release of [[neurotransmitter]]s, which in turn can change the voltage potential of downstream neurons. This change can potentially lead to even more spikes in those downstream neurons, thus passing down the signal. As many as 95% of neurons in the [[neocortex]], the outermost layer of the [[mammal]]ian [[brain]], consist of excitatory [[pyramidal cell|pyramidal neurons]],<ref>{{cite journal |title=The pyramidal neuron of the cerebral cortex: morphological and chemical characteristics of the synaptic inputs |journal=Progress in Neurobiology |year=1992 |last1=DeFelipe |first1=Javier |last2=Farinas |first2=Isabel |volume=39 |issue=6 |pages=563–607|doi=10.1016/0301-0082(92)90015-7 |pmid=1410442 |s2cid=34889543 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |title=Reconstruction and simulation of neocortical microcircuitry |journal=Cell |year=2015 |last1=Markram |first1=Henry |last2=Muller |first2=Eilif |last3=Ramaswamy |first3=Srikanth |last4=Reimann |first4=Michael |last5=Abdellah |first5=Marwan |volume=163 |issue=2 |pages=456–492|doi=10.1016/j.cell.2015.09.029 |pmid=26451489 |s2cid=14466831 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2015Cell..163..456M }}</ref> and each pyramidal neuron receives tens of thousands of inputs from other neurons.<ref>{{Citation|last1=Wong|first1=R. K. S.|title=NETWORKS {{!}} Cellular Properties and Synaptic Connectivity of CA3 Pyramidal Cells: Mechanisms for Epileptic Synchronization and Epileptogenesis|date=2009-01-01|url=http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/B9780123739612002150|encyclopedia=Encyclopedia of Basic Epilepsy Research|pages=815–819|editor-last=Schwartzkroin|editor-first=Philip A.|place=Oxford|publisher=Academic Press|language=en|doi=10.1016/b978-012373961-2.00215-0|isbn=978-0-12-373961-2|access-date=2020-11-18|last2=Traub|first2=R. D.|url-access=subscription}}</ref> Thus, spiking neurons are a major information processing unit of the [[nervous system]].

One such example of a spiking neuron model may be a highly detailed mathematical model that includes spatial [[Morphology (biology)|morphology]]. Another may be a conductance-based neuron model that views neurons as points and describes the membrane voltage dynamics as a function of trans-membrane currents. A mathematically simpler "integrate-and-fire" model significantly simplifies the description of [[ion channel]] and membrane potential dynamics (initially studied by Lapicque in 1907).<ref>{{cite journal |title=Recherches quantitatives sur l'excitation electrique des nerfs |journal=J Physiol Paris |year=1907 |last=Lapicque |first=LM |volume=9 |pages=620–635 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |title=Lapicque's introduction of the integrate-and-fire model neuron (1907) |journal=Brain Research Bulletin |year=1999 |last=Abbott |first=Larry |volume=50 |issue=5 |pages=303–304|doi=10.1016/S0361-9230(99)00161-6 |pmid=10643408 |s2cid=46170924 }}</ref>

== Biological background, classification, and aims of neuron models ==
'''Non-spiking cells, spiking cells, and their measurement'''

Not all the cells of the nervous system produce the type of spike that defines the scope of the spiking neuron models. For example, [[cochlea]]r [[hair cells]], [[Photoreceptor cell|retinal receptor cells]], and [[retinal bipolar cell]]s do not spike. Furthermore, many cells in the nervous system are not classified as neurons but instead are classified as [[Glial cell|glia]].

Neuronal activity can be measured with different experimental techniques, such as the "Whole cell" measurement technique, which captures the spiking activity of a single neuron and produces full amplitude action potentials.

With extracellular measurement techniques, one or more electrodes are placed in the [[extracellular space]]. Spikes, often from several spiking sources, depending on the size of the electrode and its proximity to the sources, can be identified with signal processing techniques. Extracellular measurement has several advantages:
* It is easier to obtain experimentally;
* It is robust and lasts for a longer time;
* It can reflect the dominant effect, especially when conducted in an anatomical region with many similar cells.

'''Overview of neuron models'''

Neuron models can be divided into two categories according to the physical units of the interface of the model. Each category could be further divided according to the abstraction/detail level:

# [[#ElectricalModels|Electrical input–output membrane voltage models]] – These models produce a prediction for membrane output voltage as a function of electrical stimulation given as current or voltage input. The various models in this category differ in the exact functional relationship between the input current and the output voltage and in the level of detail. Some models in this category predict only the moment of occurrence of the output spike (also known as "action potential"); other models are more detailed and account for sub-cellular processes. The models in this category can be either deterministic or probabilistic.
# [[#NaturalModels|Natural]] stimulus or [[#PharmacologicalModels|pharmacological input neuron models]] – The models in this category connect the input stimulus, which can be either pharmacological or natural, to the probability of a spike event. The input stage of these models is not electrical but rather has either pharmacological (chemical) concentration units, or physical units that characterize an external stimulus such as light, sound, or other forms of physical pressure. Furthermore, the output stage represents the probability of a spike event and not an electrical voltage.

Although it is not unusual in science and engineering to have several descriptive models for different abstraction/detail levels, the number of different, sometimes contradicting, biological neuron models is exceptionally high. This situation is partly the result of the many different experimental settings, and the difficulty to separate the intrinsic properties of a single neuron from measurement effects and interactions of many cells ([[Biological neural network|network]] effects).

'''Aims of neuron models'''

Ultimately, biological neuron models aim to explain the mechanisms underlying the operation of the nervous system. However, several approaches can be distinguished, from more realistic models (e.g., mechanistic models) to more pragmatic models (e.g., phenomenological models).<ref>{{Cite web|last1=Gauld|first1=Christophe|last2=Brun|first2=Cédric|last3=Boraud|first3=Thomas|last4=Carlu|first4=Mallory|last5=Depannemaecker|first5=Damien|date=2022-01-14|title=Computational Models in Neurosciences Between Mechanistic and Phenomenological Characterizations|url=https://www.preprints.org/manuscript/202201.0206/v1|doi=10.20944/preprints202201.0206.v1|s2cid=246059455 |doi-access=free }}</ref>{{better source needed|date=October 2023|reason=This pre-print is not peer reviewd and essentially self-published}} Modeling helps to analyze experimental data and address questions. Models are also important in the context of restoring lost brain functionality through [[Neuroprosthetics|neuroprosthetic]] devices.

==<span class="anchor" id="ElectricalModels"></span>Electrical input–output membrane voltage models==
The models in this category describe the relationship between neuronal membrane currents at the input stage and membrane voltage at the output stage. This category includes (generalized) integrate-and-fire models and biophysical models inspired by the work of Hodgkin–Huxley in the early 1950s using an experimental setup that punctured the cell membrane and allowed to force a specific membrane voltage/current.<ref name="Hod52" /><ref name=":6" /><ref name=":7" /><ref name=":8" />

Most modern [[#ElectricalApplications|electrical neural interfaces]] apply extra-cellular electrical stimulation to avoid membrane puncturing, which can lead to cell death and tissue damage. Hence, it is not clear to what extent the electrical neuron models hold for extra-cellular stimulation (see e.g.<ref name=":9">{{cite journal | vauthors = Mathieson K, Loudin J, Goetz G, Huie P, Wang L, Kamins TI, Galambos L, Smith R, Harris JS, Sher A, Palanker D | display-authors = 6 | title = Photovoltaic Retinal Prosthesis with High Pixel Density | journal = Nature Photonics | volume = 6 | issue = 6 | pages = 391–397 | date = June 2012 | pmid = 23049619 | pmc = 3462820 | doi = 10.1038/nphoton.2012.104 | bibcode = 2012NaPho...6..391M }}</ref>).

{{main|Hodgkin–Huxley model}}
The [[Hodgkin–Huxley model]] (H&H model)<ref name="Hod52" /><ref name=":6">{{cite journal | vauthors = Hodgkin AL, Huxley AF, Katz B | title = Measurement of current-voltage relations in the membrane of the giant axon of Loligo | journal = The Journal of Physiology | volume = 116 | issue = 4 | pages = 424–48 | date = April 1952 | pmid = 14946712 | pmc = 1392219 | doi = 10.1113/jphysiol.1952.sp004716 }}</ref><ref name=":7">{{cite journal | vauthors = Hodgkin AL, Huxley AF | title = Currents carried by sodium and potassium ions through the membrane of the giant axon of Loligo | journal = The Journal of Physiology | volume = 116 | issue = 4 | pages = 449–72 | date = April 1952 | pmid = 14946713 | pmc = 1392213 | doi = 10.1113/jphysiol.1952.sp004717 }}</ref><ref name=":8">{{cite journal | vauthors = Hodgkin AL, Huxley AF | title = The components of membrane conductance in the giant axon of Loligo | journal = The Journal of Physiology | volume = 116 | issue = 4 | pages = 473–96 | date = April 1952 | pmid = 14946714 | pmc = 1392209 | doi = 10.1113/jphysiol.1952.sp004718 }}</ref>
is a model of the relationship between the flow of ionic currents across the neuronal cell membrane and the membrane voltage of the cell.<ref name="Hod52" /><ref name=":6"/><ref name=":7"/><ref name=":8"/> It consists of a set of [[Nonlinear system#Nonlinear differential equations|nonlinear differential equations]] describing the behavior of ion channels that permeate the cell membrane of the [[squid giant axon]]. Hodgkin and Huxley were awarded the 1963 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for this work.

The voltage-current relationship, with multiple voltage-dependent currents charging the cell membrane of capacity {{math|''C''<sub>m</sub>}}

:<math>C_\mathrm{m} \frac{d V(t)}{d t} = -\sum_i I_i (t, V).</math>

The above equation is the time [[derivative]] of the law of [[Capacitor#Capacitance instability|capacitance]], {{math|''Q'' {{=}} ''CV''}} where the change of the total charge must be explained as the sum over the currents. Each current is given by

:<math>I(t,V) = g(t,V)\cdot(V-V_\mathrm{eq})</math>

where {{math|''g''(''t'',''V'')}} is the [[Electrical conductance|conductance]], or inverse resistance, which can be expanded in terms of its maximal conductance {{math|''ḡ''}} <!-- \bar{g} --> and the activation and inactivation fractions {{math|''m''}} and {{math|''h''}}, respectively, that determine how many ions can flow through available membrane channels. This expansion is given by

:<math>g(t,V)=\bar{g}\cdot m(t,V)^p \cdot h(t,V)^q</math>

and our fractions follow the first-order kinetics

:<math>\frac{d m(t,V)}{d t} = \frac{m_\infty(V)-m(t,V)}{\tau_\mathrm{m} (V)} = \alpha_\mathrm{m} (V)\cdot(1-m) - \beta_\mathrm{m} (V)\cdot m</math>

with similar dynamics for {{math|''h''}}, where we can use either {{math|''τ''}} and {{math|''m''<sub>∞</sub>}} or {{math|''α''}} and {{math|''β''}} to define our gate fractions.

The Hodgkin–Huxley model may be extended to include additional ionic currents. Typically, these include inward Ca<sup>2+</sup> and Na<sup>+</sup> input currents, as well as several varieties of K<sup>+</sup> outward currents, including a "leak" current.

The result can be at the small end of 20 parameters which one must estimate or measure for an accurate model.  In a model of a [[complex system]] of neurons, [[numerical integration]] of the equations are [[Analysis of algorithms|computationally expensive]]. Careful simplifications of the Hodgkin–Huxley model are therefore needed.

The model can be reduced to two dimensions thanks to the dynamic relations which can be established between the gating variables.<ref>{{Cite book| vauthors = Izhikevich EM |title=Dynamical systems in neuroscience: the geometry of excitability and bursting|date=2010|publisher=MIT Press|isbn=978-0-262-51420-0 |location=Cambridge, MA|oclc=457159828}}</ref> it is also possible to extend it to take into account the evolution of the concentrations (considered fixed in the original model).<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Cressman JR, Ullah G, Ziburkus J, Schiff SJ, Barreto E | title = The influence of sodium and potassium dynamics on excitability, seizures, and the stability of persistent states: I. Single neuron dynamics | journal = Journal of Computational Neuroscience | volume = 26 | issue = 2 | pages = 159–70 | date = April 2009 | pmid = 19169801 | pmc = 2704057 | doi = 10.1007/s10827-008-0132-4 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal| vauthors = Depannemaecker D, Ivanov A, Lillo D, Spek L, Bernard C, Jirsa V |title=A unified physiological framework of transitions between seizures, sustained ictal activity and depolarization block at the single neuron level |journal=Journal of Computational Neuroscience |date=2022 |volume=50 |pages=33–49 |doi=10.1007/s10827-022-00811-1 |pmid=35031915 |language=en|biorxiv=10.1101/2020.10.23.352021|pmc=8818009 }}</ref>

=== Perfect Integrate-and-fire ===
One of the earliest models of a neuron is the perfect integrate-and-fire model (also called non-leaky integrate-and-fire),  first investigated in 1907 by [[Louis Lapicque]].<ref name = "Abbott_1999">{{cite journal | vauthors = Abbott LF | title = Lapicque's introduction of the integrate-and-fire model neuron (1907) | journal = Brain Research Bulletin | volume = 50 | issue = 5–6 | pages = 303–4 | date = 1999 | pmid = 10643408 | doi = 10.1016/S0361-9230(99)00161-6 | s2cid = 46170924 | url = http://neurotheory.columbia.edu/~larry/AbbottBrResBul99.pdf | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20070613230629/http://neurotheory.columbia.edu/~larry/AbbottBrResBul99.pdf | archive-date = 2007-06-13 }}</ref> A neuron is represented by its membrane voltage {{math|''V''}} which evolves in time during stimulation with an input current {{math|''I(t)''}} according

:<math>I(t)=C \frac{d V(t)}{d t}</math>

which is just the time [[derivative]] of the law of [[Capacitor#Capacitance instability|capacitance]], {{math|''Q'' {{=}} ''CV''}}. When an input current is applied, the membrane voltage increases with time until it reaches a constant threshold {{math|''V''<sub>th</sub>}}, at which point a [[Dirac delta function|delta function]] spike occurs and the voltage is reset to its [[resting potential]], after which the model continues to run. The ''firing frequency'' of the model thus increases linearly without bound as input current increases.

The model can be made more accurate by introducing a [[refractory period (physiology)|refractory period]] {{math|''t''<sub>ref</sub>}} that limits the firing frequency of a neuron by preventing it from firing during that period. For constant input {{math|1=''I(t)=I''}} the threshold voltage is reached after an integration time {{math|1=t<sub>int</sub>=CV<sub>thr</sub>/I}} after starting from zero. After a reset, the refractory period introduces a dead time so that the total time until the next firing is {{math|''t''<sub>ref</sub>+''t''<sub>int</sub>}} . The firing frequency is the inverse of the total inter-spike interval (including dead time). The firing frequency as a function of a constant input current, is therefore

:<math>\,\! f(I)= \frac{I} {C_\mathrm{} V_\mathrm{th} + t_\mathrm{ref} I}.</math>

A shortcoming of this model is that it describes neither adaptation nor leakage.  If the model receives a below-threshold short current pulse at some time, it will retain that voltage boost forever - until another input later makes it fire. This characteristic is not in line with observed neuronal behavior. The following extensions make the integrate-and-fire model more plausible from a biological point of view.

=== Leaky integrate-and-fire ===
The leaky integrate-and-fire model, which can be traced back to [[Louis Lapicque]],<ref name = "Abbott_1999" /> contains a "leak" term in the membrane potential equation that reflects the diffusion of ions through the membrane, unlike the non-leaky integrate-and-fire model. The model equation looks like<ref name="Gerstner_2002" />

:<math>  C_\mathrm{m} \frac{d V_\mathrm{m} (t)}{d t}= I(t)-\frac{V_\mathrm{m} (t)}{R_\mathrm{m}}</math>
[[File:Leaky Integrate-and-Fire model neuron (schematic).jpg|thumb|A neuron is represented by an RC circuit with a threshold. Each input pulse (e.g. caused by a spike from a different neuron) causes a short current pulse. Voltage decays exponentially. If the threshold is reached an output spike is generated and the voltage is reset.]]
where {{math|''V''<sub>m</sub>}} is the voltage across the cell membrane and  {{math|''R''<sub>m</sub>}} is the membrane resistance. (The non-leaky integrate-and-fire model is retrieved in the limit {{math|''R''<sub>m</sub>}} to infinity, i.e. if the membrane is a perfect insulator). The model equation is valid for arbitrary time-dependent input until a threshold {{math| ''V''<sub>th</sub>}} is reached; thereafter the membrane potential is reset.

For constant input, the minimum input to reach the threshold is {{math|''I''<sub>th</sub> {{=}} ''V''<sub>th</sub> / ''R''<sub>m</sub>}}.  Assuming a reset to zero, the firing frequency thus looks like

:<math>f(I) =
\begin{cases} 
  0,  & I \le I_\mathrm{th} \\
  \left[ t_\mathrm{ref}-R_\mathrm{m} C_\mathrm{m} \log\left(1-\tfrac{V_\mathrm{th}}{I R_\mathrm{m}}\right) \right]^{-1}, & I > I_\mathrm{th} 
\end{cases} </math>

which converges for large input currents to the previous leak-free model with the refractory period.<ref name="Koch98">{{cite book| vauthors = Koch C, Segev I |title= Methods in neuronal modeling: from ions to networks|year=1999|page=687|publisher=MIT Press|location=Cambridge, Massachusetts|isbn=978-0-262-11231-4 |url= http://www.klab.caltech.edu/MNM/ |edition=2nd  |access-date=2013-01-10|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110707230906/http://www.klab.caltech.edu/MNM/|archive-date=2011-07-07}}</ref> The model can also be used for inhibitory neurons.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Brunel N | title = Dynamics of sparsely connected networks of excitatory and inhibitory spiking neurons | journal = Journal of Computational Neuroscience | volume = 8 | issue = 3 | pages = 183–208 | date = 2000-05-01 | pmid = 10809012 | doi = 10.1023/A:1008925309027 | s2cid = 1849650 }}</ref><ref name="Cejnar2020">{{cite journal | vauthors = Cejnar P, Vyšata O, Kukal J, Beránek M, Vališ M, Procházka A | title = Simple capacitor-switch model of excitatory and inhibitory neuron with all parts biologically explained allows input fire pattern dependent chaotic oscillations | journal = Scientific Reports | volume = 10 | issue = 1 | article-number = 7353 | date = April 2020 | pmid = 32355185 | pmc = 7192907 | doi = 10.1038/s41598-020-63834-7  | doi-access = free| bibcode = 2020NatSR..10.7353C }}</ref>

The most significant disadvantage of this model is that it does not contain neuronal adaptation, so that it cannot describe an experimentally measured spike train in response to constant input current.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Fuortes MG, Mantegazzini F | title = Interpretation of the repetitive firing of nerve cells | journal = The Journal of General Physiology | volume = 45 | issue = 6 | pages = 1163–79 | date = July 1962 | pmid = 13895926 | pmc = 2195242 | doi = 10.1085/jgp.45.6.1163 }}</ref> This disadvantage is removed in generalized integrate-and-fire models that also contain one or several adaptation-variables  and are able to predict spike times of cortical neurons under current injection to a high degree of accuracy.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = La Camera G, Rauch A, Lüscher HR, Senn W, Fusi S | title = Minimal models of adapted neuronal response to in vivo-like input currents | journal = Neural Computation | volume = 16 | issue = 10 | pages = 2101–24 | date = October 2004 | pmid = 15333209 | doi = 10.1162/0899766041732468 | s2cid = 1428381 }}</ref><ref name="Jolivet_2006">{{cite journal | vauthors = Jolivet R, Rauch A, Lüscher HR, Gerstner W | title = Predicting spike timing of neocortical pyramidal neurons by simple threshold models | journal = Journal of Computational Neuroscience | volume = 21 | issue = 1 | pages = 35–49 | date = August 2006 | pmid = 16633938 | doi = 10.1007/s10827-006-7074-5 | s2cid = 8911457 | url = http://infoscience.epfl.ch/record/97835 }}</ref><ref name="Pozzorini_2013">{{cite journal | vauthors = Pozzorini C, Naud R, Mensi S, Gerstner W | title = Temporal whitening by power-law adaptation in neocortical neurons | journal = Nature Neuroscience | volume = 16 | issue = 7 | pages = 942–8 | date = July 2013 | pmid = 23749146 | doi = 10.1038/nn.3431 | s2cid = 1873019 | url = http://infoscience.epfl.ch/record/189518 }}</ref>

=== Adaptive integrate-and-fire ===
{| class="wikitable" style="float:right; margin-left:15px"
|+ Experimental evidence supporting the model
!Adaptive integrate-and-fire model model
!{{Reference column heading}}
|-
|Sub-threshold voltage for time-dependent input current
|<ref name="Jolivet_2006" /><ref name="Pozzorini_2013" />
|-
|Firing times for time-dependent input current
|<ref name="Jolivet_2006" /><ref name="Pozzorini_2013" />
|-
|Firing Patterns in response to step current input 
|<ref name="Gerstner_1996" /><ref name=":17" /><ref name=":2" /> 
|}

Neuronal adaptation refers to the fact that even in the presence of a constant current injection into the soma, the intervals between output spikes increase. An adaptive integrate-and-fire neuron model combines the leaky integration of voltage {{math|''V''<sub></sub>}} with one or several adaptation variables {{math|''w''<sub>k</sub>}} (see Chapter 6.1. in the textbook Neuronal Dynamics<ref name=":12">{{cite book| vauthors = Wulfram Gerstner W, Kistler WM, Naud R, Paninski L  |title=Neuronal dynamics: from single neurons to networks and models of cognition | date = 24 July 2014 |isbn=978-1-107-06083-8|location=Cambridge, United Kingdom|oclc=861774542}}</ref>)

: <math>\tau_\mathrm{m} \frac{d V_\mathrm{m} (t)}{d t} =  R I(t)- [V_\mathrm{m} (t) - E_\mathrm{m} ]- R \sum_k w_k</math>

: <math>\tau_k \frac{d w_k (t)}{d t} = - a_k [V_\mathrm{m} (t) - E_\mathrm{m} ]- w_k + b_k \tau_k \sum_f \delta (t-t^f)
</math>

where  <math>\tau_m</math> is the membrane [[time constant]], {{math|''w''<sub>k</sub>}} is the adaptation current number, with index ''k'', <math>\tau_k</math> is the time constant of adaptation current {{math|''w''<sub>''k''</sub>}}, {{math|''E''<sub>m</sub>}} is the resting potential and {{math|''t''<sup>f</sup>}} is the firing time of the neuron and the Greek delta denotes the Dirac delta function.  Whenever the voltage reaches the firing threshold the voltage is reset to a value {{math|''V''<sub>r</sub>}} below the firing threshold. The reset value is one of the important parameters of the model. The simplest model of adaptation has only a single adaptation variable {{math|''w''<sub></sub>}} and the sum over k is removed.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Richardson MJ, Brunel N, Hakim V | title = From subthreshold to firing-rate resonance | journal = Journal of Neurophysiology | volume = 89 | issue = 5 | pages = 2538–54 | date = May 2003 | pmid = 12611957 | doi = 10.1152/jn.00955.2002 }}</ref>
[[File:Spike Time Prediction with Generalized Integrate-and-Fire model.jpg|thumb|Spike times and subthreshold voltage of cortical neuron models can be predicted by generalized integrate-and-fire models such as the adaptive integrate-and-fire model, the adaptive exponential integrate-and-fire model, or the spike response model. In the example here, adaptation is implemented by a dynamic threshold which increases after each spike.<ref name="Jolivet_2006" /><ref name="Pozzorini_2013" />]]
Integrate-and-fire neurons with one or several adaptation variables can account for a variety of neuronal firing patterns in response to constant stimulation, including adaptation, bursting, and initial bursting.<ref name="Gerstner_1996">{{cite journal | vauthors = Gerstner W, van Hemmen JL, Cowan JD | title = What matters in neuronal locking? | journal = Neural Computation | volume = 8 | issue = 8 | pages = 1653–76 | date = November 1996 | pmid = 8888612 | doi = 10.1162/neco.1996.8.8.1653 | s2cid = 1301248 | url = http://infoscience.epfl.ch/record/97772 }}</ref><ref name=":17">{{cite journal | vauthors = Izhikevich EM | title = Simple model of spiking neurons | journal = IEEE Transactions on Neural Networks | volume = 14 | issue = 6 | pages = 1569–72 | date = November 2003 | pmid = 18244602 | doi = 10.1109/TNN.2003.820440 | bibcode = 2003ITNN...14.1569I | s2cid = 814743 }}</ref><ref name=":2">{{cite journal | vauthors = Naud R, Marcille N, Clopath C, Gerstner W | title = Firing patterns in the adaptive exponential integrate-and-fire model | journal = Biological Cybernetics | volume = 99 | issue = 4–5 | pages = 335–47 | date = November 2008 | pmid = 19011922 | pmc = 2798047 | doi = 10.1007/s00422-008-0264-7 }}</ref> Moreover, adaptive integrate-and-fire neurons with several adaptation variables are able to predict spike times of cortical neurons under time-dependent current injection into the soma.<ref name="Jolivet_2006" /><ref name="Pozzorini_2013" />

=== Fractional-order leaky integrate-and-fire ===
Recent advances in computational and theoretical [[fractional calculus]] lead to a new form of model called Fractional-order leaky integrate-and-fire.<ref name=":10">{{cite journal | vauthors = Lundstrom BN, Higgs MH, Spain WJ, Fairhall AL | title = Fractional differentiation by neocortical pyramidal neurons | journal = Nature Neuroscience | volume = 11 | issue = 11 | pages = 1335–42 | date = November 2008 | pmid = 18931665 | pmc = 2596753 | doi = 10.1038/nn.2212 }}</ref><ref name="teka2014neuronal">{{cite journal | vauthors = Teka W, Marinov TM, Santamaria F | title = Neuronal spike timing adaptation described with a fractional leaky integrate-and-fire model | journal = PLOS Computational Biology | volume = 10 | issue = 3 | article-number = e1003526 | date = March 2014 | pmid = 24675903 | pmc = 3967934 | doi = 10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003526 | bibcode = 2014PLSCB..10E3526T | doi-access = free }}</ref>  An advantage of this model is that it can capture adaptation effects with a single variable. The model has the following form<ref name="teka2014neuronal" /> 
:<math>I(t)-\frac{V_\mathrm{m} (t)}{R_\mathrm{m}} = C_\mathrm{m} \frac{d^{\alpha} V_\mathrm{m} (t)}{d^{\alpha} t}</math>
Once the voltage hits the threshold it is reset. Fractional integration has been used to account for neuronal adaptation in experimental data.<ref name=":10" />

=== 'Exponential integrate-and-fire' and 'adaptive exponential integrate-and-fire' ===
{{main|Exponential integrate-and-fire}}

{| class="wikitable" style="float:right; margin-left:15px"
|+ Experimental evidence supporting the model
!Adaptive exponential integrate-and-fire
!{{Reference column heading}}
|-
|The sub-threshold current-voltage relation
|<ref name=":11">{{cite journal | vauthors = Badel L, Lefort S, Brette R, Petersen CC, Gerstner W, Richardson MJ | title = Dynamic I-V curves are reliable predictors of naturalistic pyramidal-neuron voltage traces | journal = Journal of Neurophysiology | volume = 99 | issue = 2 | pages = 656–66 | date = February 2008 | pmid = 18057107 | doi = 10.1152/jn.01107.2007 | author-link5 = Wulfram Gerstner }}</ref>
|-
|Firing patterns in response to step current input
|<ref name=":2" />
|-
|Refractoriness and adaptation
|<ref name=":15" />
|}

In the [[exponential integrate-and-fire]] model,<ref name=":19">{{cite journal | vauthors = Fourcaud-Trocmé N, Hansel D, van Vreeswijk C, Brunel N | title = How spike generation mechanisms determine the neuronal response to fluctuating inputs | journal = The Journal of Neuroscience | volume = 23 | issue = 37 | pages = 11628–40 | date = December 2003 | pmid = 14684865 | pmc = 6740955 | doi = 10.1523/JNEUROSCI.23-37-11628.2003 }}</ref> spike generation is exponential, following the equation:

: <math> \frac{dV}{dt} -  \frac{R} {\tau_m} I(t)= \frac{1} {\tau_m} \left[ E_m-V+\Delta_T \exp \left( \frac{V - V_T} {\Delta_T} \right) \right].  </math>

where <math>V</math> is the membrane potential, <math>V_T</math> is the intrinsic membrane potential threshold,  <math>\tau_m</math> is the membrane time constant, <math>E_m</math> is the resting potential, and <math>\Delta_T</math> is the sharpness of action potential initiation, usually around 1 mV for cortical pyramidal neurons.<ref name=":11" /> Once the membrane potential crosses <math>V_T</math>, it diverges to infinity in finite time.<ref name="Ostojic09">{{cite journal | vauthors = Ostojic S, Brunel N, Hakim V | title = How connectivity, background activity, and synaptic properties shape the cross-correlation between spike trains | journal = The Journal of Neuroscience | volume = 29 | issue = 33 | pages = 10234–53 | date = August 2009 | pmid = 19692598 | pmc = 6665800 | doi = 10.1523/JNEUROSCI.1275-09.2009 }}</ref> In numerical simulation the integration is stopped if the membrane potential hits an arbitrary threshold (much larger than <math>V_T</math>) at which the membrane potential is reset to a value {{math|''V''<sub>r</sub>}} . The voltage reset value {{math|''V''<sub>r</sub>}} is one of the important parameters of the model. Importantly, the right-hand side of the above equation contains a nonlinearity that can be directly extracted from experimental data.<ref name=":11" /> In this sense the exponential nonlinearity is strongly supported by experimental evidence.

In the '''adaptive exponential integrate-and-fire neuron''' <ref name=":15">{{cite journal | vauthors = Brette R, Gerstner W | title = Adaptive exponential integrate-and-fire model as an effective description of neuronal activity | journal = Journal of Neurophysiology | volume = 94 | issue = 5 | pages = 3637–42 | date = November 2005 | pmid = 16014787 | doi = 10.1152/jn.00686.2005 | url = http://infoscience.epfl.ch/record/97829 }}</ref> the above exponential nonlinearity of the voltage equation is combined with an adaptation variable w

: <math> \tau_m \frac{dV}{dt} = R I(t) + \left[ E_m-V+\Delta_T \exp \left( \frac{V - V_T} {\Delta_T} \right) \right] - R w  </math>

: <math>\tau \frac{d w (t)}{d t} = - a [V_\mathrm{m} (t) - E_\mathrm{m} ]- w + b \tau \delta (t-t^f)
</math>
[[File:Initial bursting AdEx model.png|thumb|Firing pattern of initial bursting in response to a step current input generated with the Adaptive exponential integrate-and-fire model. Other Firing patterns can also be generated.<ref name=":2" />]]
where {{math|''w''<sub></sub>}} denotes the adaptation current with time scale <math>\tau</math>. Important model parameters are the voltage reset value  {{math|''V''<sub>r</sub>}}, the intrinsic threshold <math>V_T</math>, the time constants <math>\tau</math> and <math>\tau_m</math> as well as the coupling parameters {{math|''a''<sub></sub>}} and {{math|''b''<sub></sub>}}. The adaptive exponential integrate-and-fire model inherits the experimentally derived voltage nonlinearity <ref name=":11" /> of the exponential integrate-and-fire model. But going beyond this model, it can also account for a variety of neuronal firing patterns in response to constant stimulation, including adaptation, bursting, and initial bursting.<ref name=":2" /> However, since the adaptation is in the form of a current, aberrant hyperpolarization may appear. This problem was solved by expressing it as a conductance.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Górski T, Depannemaecker D, Destexhe A | title = Conductance-Based Adaptive Exponential Integrate-and-Fire Model | journal = Neural Computation | volume = 33 | issue = 1 | pages = 41–66 | date = January 2021 | pmid = 33253029 | doi = 10.1162/neco_a_01342 | doi-access = free }}</ref>

=== Adaptive Threshold Neuron Model ===
In this model, a time-dependent function <math>\theta(t)</math> is added to the fixed threshold, <math>v_{th0}</math>, after every spike, causing an adaptation of the threshold. The [[threshold potential]], <math>v_{th}</math>, gradually returns to its steady state value depending on the threshold adaptation time constant <math>\tau_{\theta}</math>.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Neuronal Dynamics - a neuroscience textbook by Wulfram Gerstner, Werner M. Kistler, Richard Naud and Liam Paninski |url=https://neuronaldynamics.epfl.ch/ |access-date=2024-02-14 |website=neuronaldynamics.epfl.ch}}</ref> This is one of the simpler techniques to achieve spike frequency adaptation.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Ganguly |first1=Chittotosh |last2=Bezugam |first2=Sai Sukruth |last3=Abs |first3=Elisabeth |last4=Payvand |first4=Melika |last5=Dey |first5=Sounak |last6=Suri |first6=Manan |date=2024-02-01 |title=Spike frequency adaptation: bridging neural models and neuromorphic applications |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/s44172-024-00165-9.epdf?sharing_token=baTeKm8pjqSTCvHo5VF-i9RgN0jAjWel9jnR3ZoTv0PP5DkmVJjxEeRLHm3JyZz9KMIOS8SyRMFbclvN5s7WD1GususGyKXrCendPCaqURs0FlkQfsPzgm2y-O2aY0ThD0pI93ZL1_qH4Cgyb9CHyyDW05VlgSuDS2VBzR7aRU8= |journal=Communications Engineering |language=en |volume=3 |issue=1 |page=22 |doi=10.1038/s44172-024-00165-9 |issn=2731-3395|doi-access=free |pmc=11053160 }}</ref> The expression for the adaptive threshold is given by:

<math>v_{th}(t) = v_{th0} + \frac{\sum \theta(t - t_f)}{f} = v_{th0} + \frac{\sum \theta_0 \exp\left[-\frac{(t - t_f)}{\tau_{\theta}}\right]}{f}
</math>

where <math>\theta(t)</math> is defined by:  <math>\theta(t) = \theta_0 \exp\left[-\frac{t}{\tau_{\theta}}\right]</math>

When the membrane potential, <math>u(t)</math>, reaches a threshold, it is reset to <math>v_{rest}</math>:

<math>u(t) \geq v_{th}(t) \Rightarrow v(t) = v_{\text{rest}}</math>

A simpler version of this with a single time constant in threshold decay with an LIF neuron is realized in <ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Bellec |first1=Guillaume Emmanuel Fernand |last2=Salaj |first2=Darjan |last3=Subramoney |first3=Anand |last4=Legenstein |first4=Robert |last5=Maass |first5=Wolfgang |date=2018 |title=Long short-term memory and learning-to-learn in networks of spiking neurons |url=https://graz.elsevierpure.com/en/publications/long-short-term-memory-and-learning-to-learn-in-networks-of-spiki |journal=Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems|arxiv=1803.09574 }}</ref> to achieve LSTM like recurrent spiking neural networks to achieve accuracy nearer to ANNs on few spatio temporal tasks.

=== Double Exponential Adaptive Threshold (DEXAT) ===
The DEXAT neuron model is a flavor of adaptive neuron model in which the threshold voltage decays with a double exponential having two time constants. Double [[exponential decay]] is governed by a fast initial decay and then a slower decay over a longer period of time.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Shaban |first1=Ahmed |last2=Bezugam |first2=Sai Sukruth |last3=Suri |first3=Manan |date=2021-07-09 |title=An adaptive threshold neuron for recurrent spiking neural networks with nanodevice hardware implementation |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-021-24427-8.epdf?sharing_token=B7nqow9GO7Mn3wtUtni0T9RgN0jAjWel9jnR3ZoTv0Mn2mhWHZ9kJj7te4SPRRnYiLGRmiShnNugcKw2pGibEmyha-AEUKsx8rUZkjaXTjXCzcs1r_Rvzl1IkUxQ2yvO8m84pUBz7qngFo97MDzXdIXIb-R5Y7zUvcpQG8Eb6Fs= |journal=Nature Communications |language=en |volume=12 |issue=1 |page=4234 |doi=10.1038/s41467-021-24427-8  |doi-access=free|pmid=34244491 |pmc=8270926 |bibcode=2021NatCo..12.4234S |issn=2041-1723}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last1=Bezugam |first1=Sai Sukruth |last2=Shaban |first2=Ahmed |last3=Suri |first3=Manan |chapter=Neuromorphic Recurrent Spiking Neural Networks for EMG Gesture Classification and Low Power Implementation on Loihi |date=2023-05-21 |title=2023 IEEE International Symposium on Circuits and Systems (ISCAS) |publisher=IEEE |pages=1–5 |doi=10.1109/ISCAS46773.2023.10181510 |arxiv=2206.02061 |isbn=978-1-6654-5109-3|s2cid=260004324 }}</ref> This neuron used in SNNs through surrogate gradient creates an adaptive learning rate yielding higher accuracy and faster convergence, and flexible [[long short-term memory]] compared to existing counterparts in the literature. The membrane potential dynamics are described through equations and the threshold adaptation rule is:

<math>v_{th}(t) = b_{0} + \beta_{1}b_{1}(t) + \beta_{2}b_{2}(t)
</math>

The dynamics of <math>b_{1}(t)
</math> and <math>b_2(t)</math> are given by

<math>b_{1}(t + \delta t) = p_{j1}b_{1}(t) + (1 - p_{j1})z(t)\delta(t)</math>,

<math>b_{2}(t + \delta t) = p_{j2}b_{2}(t) + (1 - p_{j2})z(t)\delta(t)</math>,

where <math>p_{j1} = \exp\left[-\frac{\delta t}{\tau_{b1}}\right]</math> and <math>p_{j2} = \exp\left[-\frac{\delta t}{\tau_{b2}}\right]</math>.

Further, multi-time scale adaptive threshold neuron model showing more complex dynamics is shown in.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Kobayashi |first1=Ryota |last2=Tsubo |first2=Yasuhiro |last3=Shinomoto |first3=Shigeru |date=2009 |title=Made-to-order spiking neuron model equipped with a multi-timescale adaptive threshold |journal=Frontiers in Computational Neuroscience |volume=3 |page=9 |doi=10.3389/neuro.10.009.2009 |doi-access=free |pmid=19668702 |pmc=2722979 |issn=1662-5188}}</ref>

== Stochastic models of membrane voltage and spike timing ==
The models in this category are generalized integrate-and-fire models that include a certain level of stochasticity. Cortical neurons in experiments are found to respond reliably to time-dependent input, albeit with a small degree of variations between one trial and the next if the same stimulus is repeated.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Bryant HL, Segundo JP | title = Spike initiation by transmembrane current: a white-noise analysis | journal = The Journal of Physiology | volume = 260 | issue = 2 | pages = 279–314 | date = September 1976 | pmid = 978519 | pmc = 1309092 | doi = 10.1113/jphysiol.1976.sp011516 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Mainen ZF, Sejnowski TJ | title = Reliability of spike timing in neocortical neurons | journal = Science | volume = 268 | issue = 5216 | pages = 1503–6 | date = June 1995 | pmid = 7770778 | doi = 10.1126/science.7770778 | bibcode = 1995Sci...268.1503M }}</ref> Stochasticity in neurons has two important sources. First, even in a very controlled experiment where input current is injected directly into the soma, ion channels open and close stochastically<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Manwani A, Koch C | title = Detecting and estimating signals in noisy cable structure, I: neuronal noise sources | journal = Neural Computation | volume = 11 | issue = 8 | pages = 1797–829 | date = November 1999 | pmid = 10578033 | doi = 10.1162/089976699300015972 | s2cid = 12298894 | url = https://authors.library.caltech.edu/28336/ | access-date = 2021-04-04 | archive-date = 2021-03-07 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20210307125901/https://authors.library.caltech.edu/28336/ }}</ref> and this channel noise leads to a small amount of variability in the exact value of the membrane potential and the exact timing of output spikes. Second, for a neuron embedded in a cortical network, it is hard to control the exact input because most inputs come from unobserved neurons somewhere else in the brain.<ref name=":12" />

Stochasticity has been introduced into spiking neuron models in two fundamentally different forms: either (i) a '''noisy input''' '''current''' is added to the differential equation of the neuron model;<ref name=":21">{{cite journal | vauthors = Stein RB | title = A Theoretical Analysis of Neuronal Variability | journal = Biophysical Journal | volume = 5 | issue = 2 | pages = 173–94 | date = March 1965 | pmid = 14268952 | pmc = 1367716 | doi = 10.1016/s0006-3495(65)86709-1 | bibcode = 1965BpJ.....5..173S }}</ref> or (ii) the process of '''spike generation is noisy.'''<ref name = "Gerstner_1992">{{cite journal| vauthors = Gerstner W, van Hemmen JL |date= January 1992 |title=Associative memory in a network of 'spiking' neurons |journal=Network: Computation in Neural Systems|volume=3|issue=2|pages=139–164|doi=10.1088/0954-898X_3_2_004|issn=0954-898X|url= http://infoscience.epfl.ch/record/97753 }}</ref> In both cases, the mathematical theory can be developed for continuous time, which is then, if desired for the use in computer simulations, transformed into a discrete-time model.

The relation of noise in neuron models to the variability of spike trains and neural codes is discussed in [[Neural coding|Neural Coding]] and in Chapter 7 of the textbook Neuronal Dynamics.<ref name=":12" />

===<span class="anchor" id="Noisy input model"></span>Noisy input model (diffusive noise)===
A neuron embedded in a network receives spike input from other neurons. Since the spike arrival times are not controlled by an experimentalist they can be considered as stochastic. Thus a (potentially nonlinear) integrate-and-fire model with nonlinearity f(v) receives two inputs: an input  <math>I(t)</math> controlled by the experimentalists and a noisy input current <math>I^{\rm noise}(t)</math> that describes the uncontrolled background input.

: <math> \tau_m \frac{dV}{dt} = f(V) + R I(t) +   R I^\text{noise}(t)  </math>

'''Stein's model<ref name=":21" />''' is the special case of a leaky integrate-and-fire neuron and a stationary white noise current <math>I^{\rm noise}(t) = \xi(t)

</math> with mean zero and unit variance. In the subthreshold regime, these assumptions yield the equation of the [[Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process|Ornstein–Uhlenbeck]] process

: <math> \tau_m \frac{dV}{dt} =   [E_m-V] + R I(t) + R \xi(t)  </math>

However, in contrast to the standard Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process, the membrane voltage is reset whenever ''V'' hits the firing threshold {{math| ''V''<sub>th</sub> }}.<ref name=":21" /> Calculating the interval distribution of the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck model for constant input with threshold leads to a [[First passage time|first-passage time]] problem.<ref name=":21" /><ref name=":22">{{cite journal | vauthors = Ditlevsen S, Lansky P | title = Estimation of the input parameters in the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck neuronal model | journal = Physical Review E | volume = 71 | issue = 1 Pt 1 | article-number = 011907 | date = January 2005 | pmid = 15697630 | doi = 10.1103/PhysRevE.71.011907 | bibcode = 2005PhRvE..71a1907D }}</ref> Stein's neuron model and variants thereof have been used to fit interspike interval distributions of spike trains from real neurons under constant input current.<ref name=":22" />

In the mathematical literature, the above equation of the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process is written in the form

: <math> dV  =  [E_m-V + R I(t)] \frac{dt}{\tau_m} + \sigma \, dW  </math>

where <math>\sigma

</math> is the amplitude of the noise input and ''dW'' are increments of a [[Wiener process]]. For discrete-time implementations with time step dt the voltage updates are<ref name=":12" />

: <math> \Delta V  =  [E_m-V + R I(t)] \frac{\Delta t}{\tau_m} + \sigma \sqrt{\tau_m}y  </math>

where y is drawn from a Gaussian distribution with zero mean unit variance. The voltage is reset when it hits the firing threshold {{math| ''V''<sub>th</sub> }}.

The noisy input model can also be used in generalized integrate-and-fire models. For example, the exponential integrate-and-fire model with noisy input reads

: <math> \tau_m \frac{dV}{dt} =E_m-V+\Delta_T \exp \left( \frac{V - V_T} {\Delta_T} \right) + R  I(t) + R\xi(t)  </math>

For constant deterministic input <math>I(t)=I_0</math> it is possible to calculate the mean firing rate as a function of <math>I_0</math>.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Richardson MJ | title = Firing-rate response of linear and nonlinear integrate-and-fire neurons to modulated current-based and conductance-based synaptic drive | journal = Physical Review E | volume = 76 | issue = 2 Pt 1 | article-number = 021919 | date = August 2007 | pmid = 17930077 | doi = 10.1103/PhysRevE.76.021919 | bibcode = 2007PhRvE..76b1919R }}</ref> This is important because the frequency-current relation (f-I-curve) is often used by experimentalists to characterize a neuron.

The leaky integrate-and-fire with noisy input has been widely used in the analysis of networks of spiking neurons.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Brunel N | title = Dynamics of sparsely connected networks of excitatory and inhibitory spiking neurons | journal = Journal of Computational Neuroscience | volume = 8 | issue = 3 | pages = 183–208 | date = 2000-05-01 | pmid = 10809012 | doi = 10.1023/A:1008925309027 | s2cid = 1849650 }}</ref> Noisy input is also called 'diffusive noise' because it leads to a diffusion of the subthreshold membrane potential around the noise-free trajectory (Johannesma,<ref>{{Cite book| vauthors = Johannesma PI | chapter = Diffusion models for the stochastic activity of neurons|year=1968 |pages=116–144 | chapter-url = https://books.google.com/books?id=EsWqCAAAQBAJ&pg=PA116 | title = Neural Networks | veditors = Caianelleo ER | publisher = Springer | isbn = 978-3-642-87596-0}}</ref> The theory of spiking neurons with noisy input is reviewed in Chapter 8.2 of the textbook ''Neuronal Dynamics''.<ref name=":12" />

===<span class="anchor" id="escape rate"></span>Noisy output model (escape noise)===
In deterministic integrate-and-fire models, a spike is generated if the membrane potential {{math|''V''(t)<sub></sub>}} hits the threshold <math>V_{th}</math>. In noisy output models, the strict threshold is replaced by a noisy one as follows. At each moment in time t, a spike is generated stochastically with instantaneous stochastic intensity or [https://neuronaldynamics.epfl.ch/online/Ch9.S1.html 'escape rate'] ''<ref name=":12" />''

: <math>\rho(t) = f(V(t)-V_{th})  </math>

that depends on the momentary difference between the membrane voltage {{math|''V''(t)<sub></sub>}} and the threshold <math>V_{th}</math>.<ref name = "Gerstner_1992" /> A common choice for the '''<nowiki/>'escape rate'  <math>f</math>''' (that is consistent with biological data<ref name="Jolivet_2006" />) is

: <math> f(V-V_{th}) = \frac{1}{\tau_0} \exp[\beta(V-V_{th})]  </math>
[[File:Spike Response Model with escape noise (noisy output).jpg|thumb|Stochastic spike generation (noisy output) depends on the momentary difference between the membrane potential V(t) and the threshold. The membrane potential ''V'' of the spike response model (SRM)  has two contributions.<ref>{{Cite journal| vauthors = Gerstner W, van Hemmen JL |date=1992-01-01|title=Associative memory in a network of 'spiking' neurons|journal=Network: Computation in Neural Systems|volume=3|issue=2|pages=139–164|doi=10.1088/0954-898X_3_2_004|issn=0954-898X}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Gerstner W | title = Time structure of the activity in neural network models | journal = Physical Review E | volume = 51 | issue = 1 | pages = 738–758 | date = January 1995 | pmid = 9962697 | doi = 10.1103/PhysRevE.51.738 | bibcode = 1995PhRvE..51..738G | url = https://infoscience.epfl.ch/record/97769/files/Gerstner95PRE.pdf }}</ref> First, input current I  is filtered by a first filter k.  Second the sequence of output spikes S(t) is filtered by a second filter η and fed back. The resulting membrane V(t) potential is used to generate output spikes by a stochastic process ρ(t) with an intensity that depends on the distance between membrane potential and threshold. The spike response model (SRM) is closely related to the Generalized Linear Model (GLM).<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Truccolo W, Eden UT, Fellows MR, Donoghue JP, Brown EN | title = A point process framework for relating neural spiking activity to spiking history, neural ensemble, and extrinsic covariate effects | journal = Journal of Neurophysiology | volume = 93 | issue = 2 | pages = 1074–89 | date = February 2005 | pmid = 15356183 | doi = 10.1152/jn.00697.2004 }}</ref><ref name=":13" />]]
where <math>\tau_0</math> is a time constant that describes how quickly a spike is fired once the membrane potential reaches the threshold and <math>\beta</math> is a sharpness parameter. For <math>\beta\to\infty</math> the threshold becomes sharp and spike firing occurs deterministically at the moment when the membrane potential hits the threshold from below. The sharpness value found in experiments<ref name="Jolivet_2006" /> is <math>1/\beta\approx 4mV</math> which  means that neuronal firing becomes non-negligible as soon as the membrane potential is a few mV below the formal firing threshold.

The escape rate process via a soft threshold is reviewed in Chapter 9 of the textbook ''Neuronal Dynamics.<ref name=":12" />''

For models in discrete time, a spike is generated with probability

: <math>P_F(t_n) = F[V(t_n)-V_{th}]  </math>

that depends on the momentary difference between the membrane voltage {{math|''V''<sub></sub>}} at time <math>t_n</math> and the threshold <math>V_{th}</math>.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Weiss TF | title = A model of the peripheral auditory system | journal = Kybernetik | volume = 3 | issue = 4 | pages = 153–75 | date = November 1966 | pmid = 5982096 | doi = 10.1007/BF00290252 | s2cid = 30861035 }}</ref> The function F is often taken as a standard sigmoidal <math>F(x) = 0.5[1 + \tanh(\gamma x)]</math>  with steepness parameter <math>\gamma</math>,<ref name="Gerstner_1992" /> similar to the update dynamics in artificial neural networks. But the functional form of F can also be derived from the stochastic intensity <math>f</math> in continuous time introduced above as <math>F(y_n)\approx 1 - \exp[y_n\Delta t]</math> where <math>y_n = V(t_n)-V_{th}</math> is the threshold distance.<ref name="Gerstner_1992" />

Integrate-and-fire models with output noise can be used to predict the [[peristimulus time histogram]] (PSTH) of real neurons under arbitrary time-dependent input.<ref name="Jolivet_2006" /> For non-adaptive integrate-and-fire neurons, the interval distribution under constant stimulation can be calculated from stationary [[renewal theory]]. ''<ref name=":12" />''
