''main article'': [[Spike response model]]

The spike response model (SRM) is a [[generalized linear model]] for the subthreshold membrane voltage combined with a nonlinear output noise process for spike generation.<ref name="Gerstner_1992" /><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Gerstner W, Ritz R, van Hemmen JL | title = Why spikes? Hebbian learning and retrieval of time-resolved excitation patterns | journal = Biological Cybernetics | volume = 69 | issue = 5–6 | pages = 503–15 | date = October 1993 | pmid = 7903867 | doi = 10.1007/BF00199450 | name-list-style = vanc | s2cid = 6195748 | url = http://infoscience.epfl.ch/record/97756 }}</ref><ref name="Gerstner_2000">{{cite journal | vauthors = Gerstner W | title = Population dynamics of spiking neurons: fast transients, asynchronous states, and locking | journal = Neural Computation | volume = 12 | issue = 1 | pages = 43–89 | date = January 2000 | pmid = 10636933 | doi = 10.1162/089976600300015899 | s2cid = 7832768 | url = https://infoscience.epfl.ch/record/97797/files/Gerstner00.pdf }}</ref> The membrane voltage {{math|''V''(t)<sub></sub>}} at time ''t'' is

<math>V(t)= \sum_f \eta(t-t^f) + \int\limits_0^\infty \kappa(s) I(t-s)\,ds + V_\mathrm{rest} </math>

where {{math|''t''<sup>f</sup>}} is the firing time of spike number f of the neuron, {{math|''V''<sub>rest</sub>}} is the resting voltage in the absence of input, {{math|''I(t-s)''<sub></sub>}} is the input current at time t-s and <math>\kappa(s)</math> is a [[linear filter]] (also called kernel) that describes the contribution of an input current pulse at time t-s to the voltage at time t. The contributions to the voltage caused by a spike at time <math>t^f</math> are described by the refractory kernel <math>\eta(t-t^f)</math>.  In particular, <math>\eta(t-t^f)</math> describes the reset after the spike and the time course of the spike-afterpotential following a spike. It therefore expresses the consequences of refractoriness and adaptation.<ref name="Gerstner_1992" /><ref name="Pozzorini_2013" /> The voltage V(t) can be interpreted as the result of an integration of the differential equation of a leaky integrate-and-fire model coupled to  an arbitrary number of spike-triggered adaptation variables.<ref name="Gerstner_1996" />

Spike firing is stochastic and happens with a time-dependent stochastic intensity (instantaneous rate)

: <math> f(V-\vartheta(t)) = \frac{1}{\tau_0} \exp[\beta(V-\vartheta(t))]  </math>

with parameters <math>\tau_0</math> and <math>\beta</math> and a '''dynamic threshold''' <math>\vartheta(t)</math> given by

: <math>\vartheta(t)= \vartheta_0 + \sum_f \theta_1(t-t^f) </math>

Here <math>\vartheta_0</math> is the firing threshold of an inactive neuron and <math>\theta_1(t-t^f)</math> describes the increase of the threshold after a spike at time <math>t^f</math>.<ref name="Jolivet_2006"/><ref name="Pozzorini_2013" /> In case of a fixed threshold, one sets <math>\theta_1(t-t^f) = 0</math>. For <math>\beta \to \infty</math> the threshold process is deterministic.''<ref name=":12" />''

The time course of the filters <math>\eta,\kappa,\theta_1</math> that characterize the spike response model can be directly extracted from experimental data.<ref name="Pozzorini_2013" /> With optimized parameters the SRM describes the time course of the subthreshold  membrane voltage for time-dependent input with a precision of 2mV and can predict the timing of most output spikes with a precision of 4ms.<ref name="Jolivet_2006"/><ref name="Pozzorini_2013" /> The SRM is closely related to [[linear-nonlinear-Poisson cascade model]]s (also called Generalized Linear Model).<ref name=":13">{{cite journal | vauthors = Pillow JW, Shlens J, Paninski L, Sher A, Litke AM, Chichilnisky EJ, Simoncelli EP | title = Spatio-temporal correlations and visual signalling in a complete neuronal population | journal = Nature | volume = 454 | issue = 7207 | pages = 995–9 | date = August 2008 | pmid = 18650810 | pmc = 2684455 | doi = 10.1038/nature07140 | bibcode = 2008Natur.454..995P }}</ref> The estimation of parameters of probabilistic neuron models such as the SRM using methods developed for Generalized Linear Models<ref name=":16">{{cite journal | vauthors = Paninski L | title = Maximum likelihood estimation of cascade point-process neural encoding models | journal = Network: Computation in Neural Systems | volume = 15 | issue = 4 | pages = 243–62 | date = November 2004 | pmid = 15600233 | doi = 10.1088/0954-898X_15_4_002 | s2cid = 848548 | doi-access = free }}</ref> is discussed in Chapter 10 of the textbook ''Neuronal Dynamics''.<ref name=":12" />
[[File:Spike Response Model (schematic).jpg|thumb|Spike arrival causes postsynaptic potentials (red lines) which are summed. If the total voltage V reaches a threshold (dashed blue line) a spike is initiated (green) which also includes a spike-afterpotential. The threshold increases after each spike. Postsynaptic potentials are the response to incoming spikes while the spike-afterpotential is the response to outgoing spikes.]]
The name '''spike response model''' arises because, in a network, the input current for neuron i is  generated by the spikes of other neurons so that in the case of a network the voltage equation becomes

: <math>V_i(t)= \sum_f \eta_i(t-t_i^f)  + \sum_{j=1}^N w_{ij} \sum_{f'}\varepsilon_{ij}(t-t_j^{f'}) +  V_\mathrm{rest}  </math>

where <math>t_j^{f'}</math> is the firing times of neuron j (i.e., its spike train); <math>\eta_i(t-t^f_i)</math> describes the time course of the spike and the spike after-potential for neuron i; and <math>w_{ij}</math>  and <math>\varepsilon_{ij}(t-t_j^{f'})</math> describe the amplitude and time course of an excitatory or inhibitory '''postsynaptic potential''' (PSP) caused by the spike <math>t_j^{f'}</math> of the presynaptic neuron j. The time course <math>\varepsilon_{ij}(s)</math> of the PSP results from the convolution of the  postsynaptic current <math>I(t)</math> caused by the arrival of a presynaptic spike from neuron j with the membrane filter <math>\kappa(s)</math>.<ref name=":12" />

===<span class="anchor" id="SRM0"></span>SRM0===
The  '''SRM<small>0</small>'''<ref name="Gerstner_2000" /><ref name="Kistler_1997">{{cite journal| vauthors = Kistler WM, Gerstner W, Hemmen JL |date=1997-07-01|title=Reduction of the Hodgkin-Huxley Equations to a Single-Variable Threshold Model |journal=Neural Computation|language=en|volume=9|issue=5|pages=1015–1045|doi=10.1162/neco.1997.9.5.1015|s2cid=9861477|issn=0899-7667|url=http://infoscience.epfl.ch/record/97776}}</ref><ref name=":30">{{cite journal | vauthors = Gerstner W | title = Time structure of the activity in neural network models | journal = Physical Review E| volume = 51 | issue = 1 | pages = 738–758 | date = January 1995 | pmid = 9962697 | doi = 10.1103/PhysRevE.51.738 | bibcode = 1995PhRvE..51..738G | url = http://infoscience.epfl.ch/record/97769 }}</ref>  is a stochastic neuron model related to time-dependent nonlinear [[renewal theory]] and a simplification of the Spike Response Model (SRM). The main difference to the voltage equation of the SRM introduced above is that in the term containing the refractory kernel <math>\eta(s)</math> there is no summation sign over past spikes: only the ''most recent spike'' (denoted as the time <math>\hat{t}</math>) matters. Another difference is that the threshold is constant.  The model SRM0 can be formulated in discrete or continuous time. For example, in continuous time, the single-neuron equation is

: <math>V(t)= \eta(t-\hat{t}) + \int_0^\infty \kappa(s) I(t-s) \, ds + V_\mathrm{rest} </math>

and the network equations of the SRM<small>0</small>  are<ref name="Gerstner_2000" />

: <math>V_i(t\mid\hat{t}_i) = \eta_i(t-\hat{t}_i)   + \sum_j w_{ij} \sum_f \varepsilon_{ij}(t-\hat{t}_i,t-t^f)  +  V_\mathrm{rest} </math>

where <math>\hat{t}_i</math> is the ''last firing time neuron'' i. Note that the time course of the [[postsynaptic potential]] <math>\varepsilon_{ij}</math> is also allowed to depend on the time since the last spike of neuron i to describe a change in membrane conductance during refractoriness.<ref name="Kistler_1997" /> The instantaneous firing rate (stochastic intensity) is

: <math> f(V-\vartheta) = \frac{1}{\tau_0} \exp[\beta(V-V_{th})]  </math>

where <math>V_{th}</math> is a fixed firing threshold.  Thus spike firing of neuron i depends only on its input and the time since neuron i has fired its last spike.

With the SRM<small>0</small>, the interspike-interval distribution for constant input can be mathematically linked to the shape of the refractory kernel <math>\eta</math> .<ref name="Gerstner_1992" /><ref name="Gerstner_2000" />  Moreover the stationary frequency-current relation can be calculated from the escape rate in combination with the refractory kernel <math>\eta</math>.<ref name="Gerstner_1992" /><ref name="Gerstner_2000" /> With an appropriate choice of the kernels, the SRM<small>0</small> approximates the dynamics of the Hodgkin-Huxley model to a high degree of accuracy.<ref name="Kistler_1997" /> Moreover, the PSTH response to arbitrary time-dependent input can be predicted.<ref name="Gerstner_2000" />

== Didactic toy models of membrane voltage ==
The models in this category are highly simplified toy models that qualitatively describe the membrane voltage as a function of input. They are mainly used for didactic reasons in teaching but are not considered valid neuron models for large-scale simulations or data fitting.

=== FitzHugh–Nagumo ===
{{main|FitzHugh–Nagumo model}}
Sweeping simplifications to Hodgkin–Huxley were introduced by FitzHugh and Nagumo in 1961 and 1962. Seeking to describe "regenerative self-excitation" by a nonlinear positive-feedback membrane voltage and recovery by a linear negative-feedback gate voltage, they developed the model described by<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Fitzhugh R | title = Impulses and Physiological States in Theoretical Models of Nerve Membrane | journal = Biophysical Journal | volume = 1 | issue = 6 | pages = 445–66 | date = July 1961 | pmid = 19431309 | pmc = 1366333 | doi = 10.1016/S0006-3495(61)86902-6 | bibcode = 1961BpJ.....1..445F }}</ref>

:<math>\begin{align}{rcl}
  \dfrac{d V}{d t} &= V-V^3/3 - w + I_\mathrm{ext} \\
  \tau \dfrac{d w}{d t} &= V-a-b w
\end{align}</math>

where we again have a membrane-like voltage and input current with a slower general gate voltage {{math|''w''}} and experimentally-determined parameters {{math|''a'' {{=}} -0.7, ''b'' {{=}} 0.8, ''τ'' {{=}} 1/0.08}}. Although not derivable from biology, the model allows for a simplified, immediately available dynamic, without being a trivial simplification.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = FitzHugh R, Izhikevich E | doi = 10.4249/scholarpedia.1349 | title = FitzHugh-Nagumo model | journal = Scholarpedia | volume = 1 | issue = 9 | page = 1349 | year = 2006 | bibcode = 2006SchpJ...1.1349I | doi-access = free }}</ref> The experimental support is weak, but the model is useful as a didactic tool to introduce dynamics of spike generation through [[phase plane]] analysis. See Chapter 7 in the textbook ''Methods of Neuronal Modeling''.<ref name=":14">{{cite book|title=Methods in neuronal modeling: from ions to networks.|date=2003|publisher=Mit Press|isbn=0-262-51713-2|edition=02|location=[Place of publication not identified]|oclc=947133821}}</ref>

=== Morris–Lecar ===
{{main|Morris–Lecar model}}
In 1981, Morris and Lecar combined the Hodgkin–Huxley and FitzHugh–Nagumo models into a voltage-gated calcium channel model with a delayed-rectifier [[potassium channel]] represented by

:<math>\begin{align}
C\frac{d V}{d t} &= -I_\mathrm{ion}(V,w) + I \\
\frac{d w}{d t}  &= \varphi \cdot \frac{w_\infty - w}{\tau_{w}}
\end{align}</math>

where <math>I_\mathrm{ion}(V,w) = \bar{g}_\mathrm{Ca} m_\infty \cdot(V-V_\mathrm{Ca}) + \bar{g}_\mathrm{K} w\cdot(V-V_\mathrm{K}) + \bar{g}_\mathrm{L}\cdot(V-V_\mathrm{L})</math>.<ref name="Koch98"/> The experimental support of the model is weak, but the model is useful as a didactic tool to introduce dynamics of spike generation through [[phase plane]] analysis. See Chapter 7<ref>{{cite book | vauthors = Rinzel J, Ermentrout B | chapter = Chapter 7: Analysis of Neural Excitability and Oscillations | title = Methods in Neuronal Modeling | date = August 1998 | veditors = Segev I, Koch C | isbn = 978-0-262-51713-3 | page = 251 | publisher = MIT Press }}</ref> in the textbook ''Methods of Neuronal Modeling''.<ref name=":14" />

A two-dimensional neuron model very similar to the Morris-Lecar model can be derived step-by-step starting from the Hodgkin-Huxley model. See Chapter 4.2 in the textbook Neuronal Dynamics.<ref name=":12" />

=== Hindmarsh–Rose ===
{{main|Hindmarsh–Rose model}}
Building upon the [[FitzHugh–Nagumo model]], Hindmarsh and Rose proposed in 1984<ref name=":20">{{cite book | vauthors = Hindmarsh J, Cornelius P | chapter = The development of the hindmarsh-rose model for bursting|date=2005-10-01 | title = Bursting |pages=3–18|publisher=WORLD SCIENTIFIC|doi=10.1142/9789812703231_0001|isbn=978-981-256-506-8 }}</ref> a model of neuronal activity described by three coupled first-order differential equations:

:<math>\begin{align}
\frac{d x}{d t} &= y+3x^2-x^3-z+I \\
\frac{d y}{d t} &= 1-5x^2-y \\
\frac{d z}{d t} &= r\cdot (4(x + \tfrac{8}{5})-z)
\end{align}</math>

with {{math|''r''<sup>2</sup> {{=}} ''x''<sup>2</sup> + ''y''<sup>2</sup> + ''z''<sup>2</sup>}}, and {{math|''r'' ≈ 10<sup>−2</sup> }} so that the {{math|''z''}} variable only changes very slowly. This extra mathematical complexity allows a great variety of dynamic behaviors for the membrane potential, described by the {{math|''x''}} variable of the model, which includes chaotic dynamics. This makes the Hindmarsh–Rose neuron model very useful, because it is still simple, allows a good qualitative description of the many different firing patterns of the action potential, in particular bursting,  observed in experiments. Nevertheless, it remains a toy model and has not been fitted to experimental data. It is widely used as a reference model for bursting dynamics.<ref name=":20" />

===Theta model and quadratic integrate-and-fire ===
{{main|Theta model}}
The [[theta model]], or Ermentrout–Kopell [[canonical form|canonical]] Type I model, is mathematically equivalent to the quadratic integrate-and-fire model which in turn is an approximation to the exponential integrate-and-fire model and the Hodgkin-Huxley model. It is called a canonical model because it is one of the generic models for constant input close to the bifurcation point, which means close to the transition from silent to repetitive firing.<ref name="ErmentroutKopell1986">{{cite journal| vauthors = Ermentrout G, Kopell N |year=1986|title=Parabolic Bursting in an Excitable System Coupled with a Slow Oscillation|journal=SIAM Journal on Applied Mathematics|volume=46|issue=2|pages=233–253|doi=10.1137/0146017|issn=0036-1399}}</ref><ref name=":23">{{cite journal | vauthors = Ermentrout B | title = Type I membranes, phase resetting curves, and synchrony | journal = Neural Computation | volume = 8 | issue = 5 | pages = 979–1001 | date = July 1996 | pmid = 8697231 | doi = 10.1162/neco.1996.8.5.979 | bibcode = 1996NeCom...8..979E | s2cid = 17168880 }}</ref>

The standard formulation of the theta model is<ref name=":12" /><ref name="ErmentroutKopell1986" /><ref name=":23" />

: <math>\frac{d\theta(t)}{d t} =  (I-I_0) [1+ \cos(\theta)] + [1- \cos(\theta)]  </math>

The equation for the quadratic integrate-and-fire model is (see Chapter 5.3 in the textbook Neuronal Dynamics <ref name=":12" />)

: <math>\tau_\mathrm{m} \frac{d V_\mathrm{m} (t)}{d t} =  (I-I_0) R + [V_\mathrm{m} (t) - E_\mathrm{m} ][V_\mathrm{m} (t) - V_\mathrm{T} ] </math>

The equivalence of theta model and quadratic integrate-and-fire is for example reviewed in Chapter 4.1.2.2  of spiking neuron models.<ref name="Gerstner_2002" />

For input <math>I(t)</math> that changes over time or is far away from the bifurcation point, it is preferable to work with the exponential integrate-and-fire model (if one wants to stay in the class of one-dimensional neuron models), because real neurons exhibit the nonlinearity of the exponential integrate-and-fire model.<ref name=":11" />

==<span class="anchor" id="NaturalModels"></span> Sensory input-stimulus encoding neuron models ==

The models in this category were derived following experiments involving natural stimulation such as light, sound, touch, or odor. In these experiments, the spike pattern resulting from each stimulus presentation varies from trial to trial, but the averaged response from several trials often converges to a clear pattern. Consequently, the models in this category generate a probabilistic relationship between the input stimulus to spike occurrences. Importantly, the recorded neurons are often located several processing steps after the sensory neurons, so that these models summarize the effects of the sequence of processing steps in a compact form

=== The non-homogeneous Poisson process model (Siebert) ===
Siebert<ref name=":4">{{cite journal| vauthors = Siebert WM |date=1970-05-01|title=Frequency discrimination in the auditory system: Place or periodicity mechanisms?|journal=Proceedings of the IEEE|volume=58|issue=5|pages=723–730|doi=10.1109/PROC.1970.7727|bibcode=1970IEEEP..58..723S |issn=0018-9219}}</ref><ref name=":5">{{cite journal | vauthors = Siebert WM | title = Some implications of the stochastic behavior of primary auditory neurons | journal = Kybernetik | volume = 2 | issue = 5 | pages = 206–15 | date = June 1965 | pmid = 5839007 | doi = 10.1007/BF00306416 | s2cid = 9744183 }}</ref> modeled the neuron spike firing pattern using a non-[[homogeneous]] [[Poisson process]] model, following experiments involving the auditory system.<ref name=":4"/><ref name=":5"/> According to Siebert, the probability of a spiking event at the time interval <math>[t, t+\Delta_t]</math> is proportional to a non-negative function <math>g[s(t)]</math>, where <math>s(t)</math> is the raw stimulus.:

: <math>P_\text{spike}(t\in[t',t'+\Delta_t])=\Delta_t \cdot g[s(t)]</math>

Siebert considered several functions as <math>g[s(t)]</math>, including <math>g[s(t)] \propto s^2(t)</math> for low stimulus intensities.

The main advantage of Siebert's model is its simplicity. The shortcomings of the model is its inability to reflect properly the following phenomena:
* The transient enhancement of the neuronal firing activity in response to a step stimulus.
* The saturation of the firing rate.
* The values of inter-spike-interval-'''histogram''' at short intervals values (close to zero).
These shortcomings are addressed by the age-dependent [[point process]] model and the two-state Markov Model.<ref name="Nossenson_Messer_2010"/><ref name="NossensonMesser2012"/><ref name="NossensonMagalMesser2016"/>

===<span class="anchor" id="age-dependent model"></span>Refractoriness and age-dependent point process model===
Berry and Meister<ref>{{cite journal|vauthors=Berry MJ, Meister M|date=March 1998|title=Refractoriness and neural precision|journal=The Journal of Neuroscience|volume=18|issue=6|pages=2200–11|doi=10.1523/JNEUROSCI.18-06-02200.1998|pmc=6792934|pmid=9482804}}</ref> studied neuronal refractoriness using a stochastic model that predicts spikes as a product of two terms, a function f(s(t))  that depends on the time-dependent  stimulus s(t) and one a recovery function  <math>w(t-\hat{t}) </math> that depends on the time since the last spike

: <math>\rho(t) = f(s(t))w(t-\hat{t})  </math>

The model is also called an ''inhomogeneous Markov interval (IMI) process''.<ref name=":0">{{cite journal | vauthors = Kass RE, Ventura V | title = A spike-train probability model | journal = Neural Computation | volume = 13 | issue = 8 | pages = 1713–20 | date = August 2001 | pmid = 11506667 | doi = 10.1162/08997660152469314 | s2cid = 9909632 }}</ref>  Similar models have been used for many years in auditory neuroscience.<ref name=":1">{{cite journal | vauthors = Gaumond RP, Molnar CE, Kim DO | title = Stimulus and recovery dependence of cat cochlear nerve fiber spike discharge probability | journal = Journal of Neurophysiology | volume = 48 | issue = 3 | pages = 856–73 | date = September 1982 | pmid = 6290620 | doi = 10.1152/jn.1982.48.3.856 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Miller MI, Mark KE | title = A statistical study of cochlear nerve discharge patterns in response to complex speech stimuli | journal = The Journal of the Acoustical Society of America | volume = 92 | issue = 1 | pages = 202–9 | date = July 1992 | pmid = 1324958 | doi = 10.1121/1.404284 | bibcode = 1992ASAJ...92..202M }}</ref><ref name="The transmission of signals by audi">{{cite journal | vauthors = Johnson DH, Swami A | title = The transmission of signals by auditory-nerve fiber discharge patterns | journal = The Journal of the Acoustical Society of America | volume = 74 | issue = 2 | pages = 493–501 | date = August 1983 | pmid = 6311884 | doi = 10.1121/1.389815 | bibcode = 1983ASAJ...74..493J }}</ref> Since the model keeps memory of the last spike time it is non-Poisson and falls in the class of time-dependent renewal models.<ref name=":12" /> It is closely related to the model  [[#SRM0|SRM0]] with exponential escape rate.<ref name=":12" /> Importantly, it is possible to fit parameters of the age-dependent point process model so as to describe not just the PSTH response, but also the interspike-interval statistics.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1" /><ref name="The transmission of signals by audi"/>

=== Linear-nonlinear Poisson cascade model and GLM ===
{{Main|Linear-nonlinear-Poisson cascade model}}
The [[linear-nonlinear-Poisson cascade model]] is a cascade of a linear filtering process followed by a nonlinear spike generation step.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Chichilnisky EJ | title = A simple white noise analysis of neuronal light responses | journal = Network: Computation in Neural Systems | volume = 12 | issue = 2 | pages = 199–213 | date = May 2001 | pmid = 11405422 | doi = 10.1080/713663221 }}</ref> In the case that output spikes feed back, via a linear filtering process, we arrive at a model that is known in the neurosciences as Generalized Linear Model (GLM).<ref name=":13" /><ref name=":16" /> The GLM is mathematically equivalent to the spike response model SRM) with  escape noise; but whereas in the SRM the internal variables are interpreted as the membrane potential and the firing threshold,  in the GLM the internal variables are abstract quantities that summarizes the net effect of input (and recent output spikes) before spikes are generated in the final step.<ref name=":12" /><ref name=":13" />

===<span class="anchor" id="NossensonMesserModel"></span><span class="anchor" id="NossensonMesserModel2"></span>The two-state Markov model (Nossenson & Messer)===

The spiking neuron model by Nossenson & Messer<ref name="Nossenson_Messer_2010">{{cite book |doi = 10.1109/SAM.2010.5606761|chapter = Modeling neuron firing pattern using a two-state Markov chain|title = 2010 IEEE Sensor Array and Multichannel Signal Processing Workshop|year = 2010| vauthors = Nossenson N, Messer H  |isbn = 978-1-4244-8978-7|s2cid = 10973225}}</ref><ref name="NossensonMesser2012">{{cite journal | vauthors = Nossenson N, Messer H | title = Optimal sequential detection of stimuli from multiunit recordings taken in densely populated brain regions | journal = Neural Computation | volume = 24 | issue = 4 | pages = 895–938 | date = April 2012 | pmid = 22168560 | doi = 10.1162/NECO_a_00257 | s2cid = 16994688 }}</ref><ref name="NossensonMagalMesser2016">{{cite journal | vauthors = Nossenson N, Magal N, Messer H | journal = Neurocomputing | title = Detection of stimuli from multi-neuron activity: Empirical study and theoretical implications. | date = 2016 | volume = 174 | pages = 822–837 | doi = 10.1016/j.neucom.2015.10.007 }}</ref> produces the probability of the neuron firing a spike as a function of either an external or pharmacological stimulus.<ref name="Nossenson_Messer_2010"/><ref name="NossensonMesser2012"/><ref name="NossensonMagalMesser2016"/> The model consists of a cascade of a receptor layer model and a spiking neuron model, as shown in Fig 4. The connection between the external stimulus to the spiking probability is made in two steps: First, a receptor cell model translates the raw external stimulus to neurotransmitter concentration, and then, a spiking neuron model connects neurotransmitter concentration to the firing rate (spiking probability).  Thus, the spiking neuron model by itself depends on neurotransmitter concentration at the input stage.<ref name="Nossenson_Messer_2010"/><ref name="NossensonMesser2012"/><ref name="NossensonMagalMesser2016"/>
[[File:Nerve model 2wiki.png|thumb|400px|Fig 4: High level block diagram of the receptor layer and neuron model by Nossenson & Messer.<ref name="Nossenson_Messer_2010"/><ref name="NossensonMagalMesser2016"/>]]
[[File:Firing rate improved.png|thumb|400px|Fig 5. The prediction for the firing rate in response to a pulse stimulus as given by the model by Nossenson & Messer.<ref name="Nossenson_Messer_2010"/><ref name="NossensonMagalMesser2016"/>]]
An important feature of this model is the prediction for neurons firing rate pattern which captures, using a low number of free parameters, the characteristic edge emphasized response of neurons to a stimulus pulse, as shown in Fig. 5. The firing rate is identified both as a normalized probability for neural spike firing and as a quantity proportional to the current of neurotransmitters released by the cell. The expression for the firing rate takes the following form:

: <math>R_\text{fire}(t)=\frac{P_\text{spike}(t;\Delta_t)}{\Delta_t}=[y(t)+R_0] \cdot P_0(t)</math>

where, 
* P0 is the probability of the neuron being "armed" and ready to fire. It is given by the following differential equation:

: <math>\dot{P}_0=-[y(t)+R_0+R_1] \cdot P_0(t) +R_1</math>

P0 could be generally calculated recursively using the Euler method, but in the case of a pulse of stimulus, it yields a simple closed-form expression.<ref name="Nossenson_Messer_2010" /><ref name="NossensonPhD2013">{{cite thesis|url=http://primage.tau.ac.il/libraries/theses/exeng/free/2531730.pdf|title=Model Based Detection of a Stimulus Presence from Neurophysiological Signals|vauthors=Nossenson N|degree=Ph.D.|publisher=University of Tel-Aviv|year=2013|location=The Neiman Library of Exact Sciences & Engineering, Tel Aviv University|access-date=2016-04-12|archive-date=2017-03-05|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170305015246/http://primage.tau.ac.il/libraries/theses/exeng/free/2531730.pdf}}</ref>
* ''y''(''t'') is the input of the model and is interpreted as the neurotransmitter concentration on the cell surrounding (in most cases glutamate). For an external stimulus it can be estimated through the receptor layer model:

: <math>y(t) \simeq   g_\text{gain} \cdot \langle s^2(t)\rangle,</math>

with <math>\langle s^2(t)\rangle </math> being a short temporal average of stimulus power (given in Watt or other energy per time unit).
* ''R''<sub>0</sub> corresponds to the intrinsic spontaneous firing rate of the neuron.
* ''R''<sub>1</sub> is the recovery rate of the neuron from the refractory state.

Other predictions by this model include:

1) The averaged evoked response potential (ERP) due to the population of many neurons in unfiltered measurements resembles the firing rate.<ref name="NossensonMagalMesser2016"/>

2) The voltage variance of activity due to multiple neuron activity resembles the firing rate (also known as Multi-Unit-Activity power or MUA).<ref name="NossensonMesser2012"/><ref name="NossensonMagalMesser2016"/>

3) The inter-spike-interval probability distribution takes the form a gamma-distribution like function.<ref name="Nossenson_Messer_2010" /><ref name="NossensonPhD2013" />

== <span class="anchor" id="PharmacologicalModels"></span> Pharmacological input stimulus neuron models ==
The models in this category produce predictions for experiments involving pharmacological stimulation.

=== Synaptic transmission (Koch & Segev)===
{{see also|Neurotransmission}}
According to the model by Koch and Segev,<ref name="Koch98"/> the response of a neuron to individual neurotransmitters can be modeled as an extension of the classical Hodgkin–Huxley model with both standard and nonstandard kinetic currents. Four neurotransmitters primarily influence the CNS. [[AMPA receptor|AMPA/kainate receptors]] are fast [[Excitatory synapse|excitatory]] mediators while [[NMDA receptor]]s mediate considerably slower currents. Fast [[Inhibitory synapse|inhibitory]] currents go through [[GABAA receptor|GABA<sub>A</sub> receptors]], while [[GABAB receptor|GABA<sub>B</sub> receptors]] mediate by secondary ''G''-protein-activated potassium channels. This range of mediation produces the following current dynamics:

*<math>I_\mathrm{AMPA}(t,V) = \bar{g}_\mathrm{AMPA} \cdot [O] \cdot (V(t)-E_\mathrm{AMPA})</math>
*<math>I_\mathrm{NMDA}(t,V) = \bar{g}_\mathrm{NMDA} \cdot B(V) \cdot [O] \cdot (V(t)-E_\mathrm{NMDA})</math>
*<math>I_\mathrm{GABA_A}(t,V) = \bar{g}_\mathrm{GABA_A} \cdot ([O_1]+[O_2]) \cdot (V(t)-E_\mathrm{Cl})</math>
*<math>I_\mathrm{GABA_B}(t,V) = \bar{g}_\mathrm{GABA_B} \cdot \tfrac{[G]^n}{[G]^n+K_\mathrm{d}} \cdot (V(t)-E_\mathrm{K})</math>

where {{math|''ḡ''}} <!-- \bar{g} --> is the maximal<ref name="Hod52">{{cite journal | vauthors = Hodgkin AL, Huxley AF | title = A quantitative description of membrane current and its application to conduction and excitation in nerve | journal = The Journal of Physiology | volume = 117 | issue = 4 | pages = 500–44 | date = August 1952 | pmid = 12991237 | pmc = 1392413 | doi = 10.1113/jphysiol.1952.sp004764 }}</ref><ref name="Koch98" /> conductance (around 1[[Siemens (unit)|S]]) and {{math|''E''}} is the equilibrium potential of the given ion or transmitter (AMDA, NMDA, [[Chlorine|Cl]], or [[Potassium|K]]), while {{math|[''O'']}} describes the fraction of open receptors. For NMDA, there is a significant effect of ''magnesium block'' that depends [[sigmoid function|sigmoidally]] on the concentration of intracellular magnesium by {{math|''B''(''V'')}}. For GABA<sub>B</sub>, {{math|[''G'']}} is the concentration of the ''G''-protein, and {{math|''K''<sub>d</sub>}} describes the dissociation of ''G'' in binding to the potassium gates.

The dynamics of this more complicated model have been well-studied experimentally and produce important results in terms of very quick [[synaptic plasticity|synaptic potentiation and depression]], that is fast, short-term learning.

The stochastic '''model by Nossenson and Messer''' translates neurotransmitter concentration at the input stage to the probability of releasing neurotransmitter at the output stage.<ref name="Nossenson_Messer_2010" /><ref name="NossensonMesser2012"/><ref name="NossensonMagalMesser2016"/> For a more detailed description of this model, see the [[#NossensonMesserModel2|Two state Markov model section]] above.

== HTM neuron model ==
The HTM neuron model was developed by [[Jeff Hawkins]] and researchers at Numenta and is based on a theory called [[Hierarchical Temporal Memory]], originally described in the book ''[[On Intelligence]]''. It is based on [[neuroscience]] and the physiology and interaction of [[pyramidal neurons]] in the [[neocortex]] of the human brain. <br />
[[File:Neuron comparison.png|thumb|upright=1.7|500px|Comparing the [[artificial neural network]] (A), the biological neuron (B), and the HTM neuron (C)]]

        {| class="wikitable"
        | {{center|'''Artificial Neural Network (ANN)'''}}
        | {{center|'''Neocortical Pyramidal Neuron (Biological Neuron)'''}}
        | {{center|'''HTM Model Neuron'''}}
        |-
        | - Few synapses

- No dendrites

- Sum input x weights

- Learns by modifying the weights of synapses
        | - Thousands of synapses on the dendrites

- Active dendrites: cell recognizes hundreds of unique patterns

- Co-activation of a set of synapses on a dendritic segment causes an NMDA spike and depolarization at the soma

- Sources of input to the cell:
# Feedforward inputs that form synapses proximal to the soma and directly lead to action potentials
# NMDA spikes generated in the more distal basal
# Apical dendrites that depolarize the soma (usually insufficient to generate a somatic action potential)

- Learns by growing new synapses
        | - Inspired by the pyramidal cells in neocortex layers 2/3 and 5

- Thousands of synapses

- Active dendrites: cell recognizes hundreds of unique patterns

- Models dendrites and NMDA spikes with each array of coincident detectors having a set of synapses

- Learns by modeling the growth of new synapses
        |}

== Relation between artificial and biological neuron models ==
The most basic model of a neuron consists of an input with some [[synaptic weight]] vector and an [[activation function]] or [[transfer function]] inside the neuron determining output. This is the basic structure used for artificial neurons, which in a [[artificial neural network|neural network]] often looks like

: <math>y_i = \varphi\left( \sum_j w_{ij} x_j \right)</math>

where {{math|''y''<sub>''i''</sub>}} is the output of the {{math|''i''}} th neuron, {{math|''x''<sub>''j''</sub>}} is the {{math|''j''}}th input neuron signal, {{math|''w''<sub>''ij''</sub>}} is the synaptic weight (or strength of connection) between the neurons {{math|''i''}} and {{math|''j''}}, and {{math|''φ''}} is the [[activation function]]. While this model has seen success in machine-learning applications, it is a poor model for real (biological) neurons, because it lacks time-dependence  in input and output.

When an input is switched on at a time t and kept constant thereafter, biological neurons emit a spike train. Importantly, this spike train is not regular but exhibits a temporal structure characterized by adaptation, bursting, or initial bursting followed by regular spiking. Generalized integrate-and-fire models such as the Adaptive Exponential Integrate-and-Fire model, the spike response model, or the (linear) adaptive integrate-and-fire model can capture these neuronal firing patterns.<ref name="Gerstner_1996" /><ref name=":17" /><ref name=":2" />

Moreover, neuronal input in the brain is time-dependent. Time-dependent input is transformed by complex linear and nonlinear filters into a spike train in the output. Again, the spike response model or the adaptive integrate-and-fire model enables to prediction of the spike train in the output for arbitrary time-dependent input,<ref name="Jolivet_2006" /><ref name="Pozzorini_2013" /> whereas an [[artificial neuron]] or a simple leaky integrate-and-fire does not.

If we take the Hodkgin-Huxley model as a starting point, generalized integrate-and-fire models can be derived systematically in a step-by-step simplification procedure. This has been shown explicitly for the [[exponential integrate-and-fire]]<ref name=":19" /> model and the [[spike response model]].<ref name="Kistler_1997" />

In the case of modeling a biological neuron, physical analogs are used in place of abstractions such as "weight" and "transfer function". A neuron is filled and surrounded with water-containing ions, which carry electric charge. The neuron is bound by an insulating cell membrane and can maintain a concentration of charged ions on either side that determines a [[capacitance]] {{math|''C''<sub>m</sub>}}. The firing of a neuron involves the movement of ions into the cell, that occurs when [[neurotransmitters]] cause [[ion channels]] on the cell membrane to open. We describe this by a physical time-dependent [[Electric current|current]] {{math|''I''(''t'')}}. With this comes a change in [[voltage]], or the electrical potential energy difference between the cell and its surroundings, which is observed to sometimes result in a [[voltage spike]] called an [[action potential]] which travels the length of the cell and triggers the release of further neurotransmitters. The voltage, then, is the quantity of interest and is given by {{math|''V''<sub>m</sub>(''t'')}}.<ref name="Cejnar2020" />

If the input current is constant, most neurons emit after some time of adaptation or initial bursting a regular spike train. The frequency of regular firing in response to a constant current {{math|''I''}} is described by the frequency-current relation, which corresponds to the transfer function <math>\varphi</math> of artificial neural networks. Similarly, for all spiking neuron models, the transfer function <math>\varphi</math> can be calculated numerically (or analytically).

== Cable theory and compartmental models ==

{{see also |Cable theory}}

All of the above deterministic models are point-neuron models because they do not consider the spatial structure of a neuron. However, the dendrite contributes to transforming input into output.<ref name=":18">{{cite journal | vauthors = Hay E, Hill S, Schürmann F, Markram H, Segev I | title = Models of neocortical layer 5b pyramidal cells capturing a wide range of dendritic and perisomatic active properties | journal = PLOS Computational Biology | volume = 7 | issue = 7 | article-number = e1002107 | date = July 2011 | pmid = 21829333 | pmc = 3145650 | doi = 10.1371/journal.pcbi.1002107 | bibcode = 2011PLSCB...7E2107H | doi-access = free }}</ref><ref name=":14" />  Point neuron models are valid description in three cases. (i) If input current is directly injected into the soma. (ii) If synaptic input arrives predominantly at or close to the soma (closeness is defined by a length scale <math>\lambda</math> introduced below.  (iii) If synapse arrives anywhere on the dendrite, but the dendrite is completely linear. In the last case, the cable acts as a linear filter; these linear filter properties can be included in the formulation of generalized integrate-and-fire models such as the [[spike response model]].

The filter properties can be calculated from a [[Cable theory|cable equation]].

Let us consider a cell membrane in the form of a cylindrical cable. The position on the cable is denoted by x and the voltage across the cell membrane by V. The cable is characterized by a longitudinal resistance  <math>r_l</math>  per unit length and a membrane resistance <math>r_m</math> . If everything is linear, the voltage changes as a function of time{{NumBlk|:|<math>\frac{r_m}{r_l} \frac{\partial ^2 V}{\partial x^2}=c_m r_m \frac{\partial V}{\partial t}+ V</math>|{{EquationRef|19}}}}We introduce a length scale  <math>\lambda^2 = {r_m}/{r_l}</math> on the left side and time constant  <math>\tau = c_m r_m</math> on the right side. The [[cable equation]] can now be written in its perhaps best-known form: {{NumBlk|:|<math>\lambda^2 \frac{\partial ^2 V}{\partial x^2}=\tau \frac{\partial V}{\partial t}+ V</math>|{{EquationRef|20}}}}
The above cable equation is valid for a single cylindrical cable.

Linear cable theory describes the [[dendrites|dendritic arbor]] of a neuron as a cylindrical structure undergoing a regular pattern of [[Bifurcation theory|bifurcation]], like branches in a tree. For a single cylinder or an entire tree, the static input conductance at the base (where the tree meets the cell body or any such boundary) is defined as

:<math>G_{in} = \frac{G_\infty \tanh(L) + G_L}{1+(G_L / G_\infty )\tanh(L)}</math>,

where {{math|''L''}} is the electrotonic length of the cylinder, which depends on its length, diameter, and resistance. A simple recursive algorithm scales linearly with the number of branches and can be used to calculate the effective conductance of the tree. This is given by

:<math>\,\! G_D = G_m A_D \tanh(L_D) / L_D</math>

where {{math|''A''<sub>''D''</sub> {{=}} ''πld''}} is the total surface area of the tree of total length {{math|''l''}}, and {{math|''L''<sub>''D''</sub>}} is its total electrotonic length. For an entire neuron in which the cell body conductance is {{math|''G''<sub>''S''</sub>}} and the membrane conductance per unit area is {{math|''G''<sub>''md''</sub> {{=}} ''G''<sub>''m''</sub> / ''A''}}, we find the total neuron conductance {{math|''G''<sub>''N''</sub>}} for {{math|''n''}} dendrite trees by adding up all tree and soma conductances, given by

:<math>G_N = G_S + \sum_{j=1}^n A_{D_j} F_{dga_j},</math>

where we can find the general correction factor {{math|''F''<sub>''dga''</sub>}} experimentally by noting {{math|''G''<sub>''D''</sub> {{=}} ''G''<sub>''md''</sub>''A''<sub>''D''</sub>''F''<sub>''dga''</sub>}}.

The linear cable model makes several simplifications to give closed analytic results, namely that the dendritic arbor must branch in diminishing pairs in a fixed pattern and that dendrites are linear. A compartmental model<ref name=":14" /> allows for any desired tree topology with arbitrary branches and lengths, as well as arbitrary nonlinearities. It is essentially a discretized computational implementation of nonlinear dendrites.

Each piece, or compartment, of a dendrite, is modeled by a straight cylinder of arbitrary length {{math|''l''}} and diameter {{math|''d''}} which connects with fixed resistance to any number of branching cylinders. We define the conductance ratio of the {{math|''i''}}th cylinder as {{math|''B''<sub>''i''</sub> {{=}} ''G''<sub>''i''</sub> / ''G''<sub>∞</sub>}}, where <math>G_\infty=\tfrac{\pi d^{3/2}}{2\sqrt{R_i R_m}}</math> and {{math|''R''<sub>''i''</sub>}} is the resistance between the current compartment and the next. We obtain a series of equations for conductance ratios in and out of a compartment by making corrections to the normal dynamic {{math|''B''<sub>out,''i''</sub> {{=}} ''B''<sub>in,''i+1''</sub>}}, as

*<math>B_{\mathrm{out},i} = \frac{B_{\mathrm{in},i+1}(d_{i+1}/d_i)^{3/2} }{ \sqrt{R_{\mathrm{m},i+1}/R_{\mathrm{m},i}} }</math>
*<math>B_{\mathrm{in},i} = \frac{ B_{\mathrm{out},i} + \tanh X_i }{ 1+B_{\mathrm{out},i}\tanh X_i }</math>
*<math>B_\mathrm{out,par} = \frac{B_\mathrm{in,dau1} (d_\mathrm{dau1}/d_\mathrm{par})^{3/2}} {\sqrt{R_\mathrm{m,dau1}/R_\mathrm{m,par}}} + \frac{B_\mathrm{in,dau2} (d_\mathrm{dau2}/d_\mathrm{par})^{3/2}} {\sqrt{R_\mathrm{m,dau2}/R_\mathrm{m,par}}} + \ldots</math>

where the last equation deals with ''parents'' and ''daughters'' at branches, and <math>X_i = \tfrac{l_i \sqrt{4R_i}}{\sqrt{d_i R_m}}</math>. We can iterate these equations through the tree until we get the point where the dendrites connect to the cell body (soma), where the conductance ratio is {{math|''B''<sub>in,stem</sub>}}. Then our total neuron conductance for static input is given by

:<math>G_N = \frac{A_\mathrm{soma}}{R_\mathrm{m,soma}} + \sum_j B_{\mathrm{in,stem},j} G_{\infty,j}.</math>

Importantly, static input is a very special case. In biology, inputs are time-dependent. Moreover, dendrites are not always linear.

Compartmental models enable to include nonlinearities via ion channels positioned at arbitrary locations along the dendrites.<ref name=":18" /><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Markram H, Muller E, ==Conjectures regarding the role of the neuron in the wider context of the brain principle of operation ==

=== The neurotransmitter-based energy detection scheme ===
The neurotransmitter-based energy detection scheme<ref name="NossensonMagalMesser2016" /><ref name="NossensonPhD2013" /> suggests that the neural tissue chemically executes a Radar-like detection procedure.

[[File:Neural detector nossenson 2013.png|thumb|611x411px|Fig. 6 The biological neural detection scheme as suggested by Nossenson et al.<ref name="NossensonMagalMesser2016" /><ref name="NossensonPhD2013" />]]

As shown in Fig. 6, the key idea of the conjecture is to account for neurotransmitter concentration, neurotransmitter generation, and neurotransmitter removal rates as the important quantities in executing the detection task, while referring to the measured electrical potentials as a side effect that only in certain conditions coincide with the functional purpose of each step.  The detection scheme is similar to a radar-like "energy detection" because it includes signal squaring, temporal summation, and a threshold switch mechanism, just like the energy detector, but it also includes a unit that emphasizes stimulus edges and a variable memory length (variable memory). According to this conjecture, the physiological equivalent of the energy test statistics is neurotransmitter concentration, and the firing rate corresponds to neurotransmitter current. The advantage of this interpretation is that it leads to a unit-consistent explanation which allows for bridge between electrophysiological measurements, biochemical measurements, and psychophysical results.

The evidence reviewed in<ref name="NossensonMagalMesser2016" /><ref name="NossensonPhD2013" /> suggests the following association between functionality to histological classification:
# Stimulus squaring is likely to be performed by receptor cells.
# Stimulus edge emphasizing and signal transduction is performed by neurons.
# Temporal accumulation of neurotransmitters is performed by glial cells. Short-term neurotransmitter accumulation is likely to occur also in some types of neurons.
# Logical switching is executed by glial cells, and it results from exceeding a threshold level of neurotransmitter concentration. This threshold crossing is also accompanied by a change in neurotransmitter leak rate.
# Physical all-or-non movement switching is due to muscle cells and results from exceeding a certain neurotransmitter concentration threshold on muscle surroundings.

Note that although the electrophysiological signals in Fig.6 are often similar to the functional signal (signal power/neurotransmitter concentration / muscle force), there are some stages in which the electrical observation differs from the functional purpose of the corresponding step. In particular, Nossenson et al. suggested that glia threshold crossing has a completely different functional operation compared to the radiated electrophysiological signal and that the latter might only be a side effect of glia break.

==General comments regarding the modern perspective of scientific and engineering models==
* The models above are still idealizations. Corrections must be made for the increased membrane surface area given by numerous dendritic spines, temperatures significantly hotter than room-temperature experimental data, and nonuniformity in the cell's internal structure.<ref name="Koch98"/> Certain observed effects do not fit into some of these models. For instance, the temperature cycling (with minimal net temperature increase) of the cell membrane during action potential propagation is not compatible with models that rely on modeling the membrane as a resistance that must dissipate energy when current flows through it. The transient thickening of the cell membrane during action potential propagation is also not predicted by these models, nor is the changing capacitance and voltage spike that results from this thickening incorporated into these models. The action of some anesthetics such as inert gases is problematic for these models as well. New models, such as the [[soliton model]] attempt to explain these phenomena, but are less developed than older models and have yet to be widely applied.
* Modern views regarding the role of the scientific model suggest that "All models are wrong but some are useful" (Box and Draper, 1987, Gribbin, 2009; Paninski et al., 2009).
*Recent conjecture suggests that each neuron might function as a collection of independent threshold units. It is suggested that a neuron could be anisotropically activated following the origin of its arriving signals to the membrane, via its dendritic trees. The spike waveform was also proposed to be dependent on the origin of the stimulus.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Sardi S, Vardi R, Sheinin A, Goldental A, Kanter I | title = New Types of Experiments Reveal that a Neuron Functions as Multiple Independent Threshold Units | language = En | journal = Scientific Reports | volume = 7 | issue = 1 | article-number = 18036 | date = December 2017 | pmid = 29269849 | pmc = 5740076 | doi = 10.1038/s41598-017-18363-1  | doi-access = free| bibcode = 2017NatSR...718036S }}</ref>
